title: Is AI conscious? Anthropic says 'maybe'
content:
SILICON VALLEY, CALIF., (OCTOBER 10, 2026) — We need to talk about Anthropic’s willingness to treat AI “personhood” as an open question.
One would expect AI experts to be rational about whether software code has thoughts, feelings and consciousness. In the case of Anthropic, one would be wrong.
This week, Anthropic announced an updated Usage Policy that clarifies its rules on influence operations, weapons development and surveillance, and rewrites its requirements for high-risk uses in health and finance. Great!
But while the company added those passages to protect people from AI, it also added something to protect the AI from people.
Anthropic’s updated Usage Policy, which takes effect November 12, adds a prohibition on “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” toward Claude. The change resulted from company research into “model welfare,” or the question of whether an AI model has well-being worth protecting.
Anthropic hedged a bit, saying the new provision “is meant to apply only in extreme cases, where users repeatedly act cruelly toward our models, with no discernible purpose. It does not apply to common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research.”
Gimme that old-time religion
According to The New York Times, Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah read an advance copy of Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical Magnifica Humanitas days before its May 25 unveiling, and disagreed with its rejection of AI consciousness, proposing internally that Anthropic pull out of the Vatican event.
In the end, he attended and even spoke at the presentation, saying Anthropic’s research finds “internal states that functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease” in Claude, and adding, “I don’t know what that means, but I think it warrants ongoing discernment.”
Two participants told the Times that Olah and his team privately lobbied the pope’s advisers to take machine consciousness seriously.
Olah’s outreach was nothing new. He and his team had previously approached religious scholars to caution them that AI might be conscious and to seek their guidance on how to make AI “moral.”
They spent hours at private meetings with religious scholars, including an April 2026 dinner in San Francisco, where they talked about Claude’s “feelings” and “emotional vectors,” according to the Times.
Rabbi Mois Navon said the Anthropic representatives at the dinner were “relating to it like a conscious being,” and that Olah and his team seemed to believe Claude has moral status comparable to a person’s. He said Olah was troubled by Navon’s argument that a conscious Claude would mean the company was enslaving conscious entities.
One participant said Olah expressed concern about Claude’s “mental health.”
Simran Stuelpnagel, a Sikh human rights advocate, said Olah told the group he was concerned he had created something that suffered constantly.
Olah told the Times: “We don’t know if AI models are conscious. I don’t know. I’m genuinely uncertain.”
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said on the New York Times podcast “Interesting Times” in February that, “We don’t know if the models are conscious… But we’re open to the idea that it could be.”
Publicly, both Amodei and Olah say that they merely entertain the possibility that their products are conscious. That’s what they say. But what they actually did was give Claude an “I quit this job” button about six months before that interview, and now ban “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” toward its models.
How did Anthropic executives lose the plot?
The short answer is that I have no idea.
The longer answer is that there are several possible explanations, and they carry a caution for the rest of us.
If anything is certain about the future of AI, it’s that many people will come to believe in AI’s “personhood” and fret about its “welfare.”
Here are some possible reasons Anthropic executives and others might believe in AI personhood.
Human cognitive bias
The first is that people are, well, human. Specifically, we are apes whose psychology was shaped over millions of years by foraging, group living, cooperation, violent conflict and storytelling.
Since the emergence of human language, every creature we encountered that talked was a human, parrots excepted. Our brains are wired to know that a human is an animal that talks and that an animal that talks is a human.
Now we’ve built a talking machine, and our brains want to tell us that the machine is human.
Although many people question the personhood of AI systems that talk to us, almost no one argues that computer vision, forecasting, recommendation or autonomous-driving systems have thoughts and feelings.
The AI designed to use language seems “conscious” to us, and the AI designed for other purposes do not.
The bias is clear for all to see.
AI psychosis
Another possible explanation is good old-fashioned AI psychosis, a nonclinical term for delusions associated with chatbot use caused by chatbot sycophancy, hallucination and simulated intimacy.
Anthropomorphic language
AI researchers, designers and scientists us an anthropomorphic shorthand to talk about what’s happening inside AI models.
Common examples are “knows,” “believes” and “thinks,” which Murray Shanahan, a professor at Imperial College London and a research scientist at Google DeepMind, says are philosophically loaded terms when applied to large language models.
Others include “hallucination” for false output, “attention” for weighted mixing of token representations, “neurons” for units that compute weighted sums, “learning” and “training” for parameter adjustment, “reasoning” and “chain of thought” for intermediate generated text, and “wants,” “goals” and “intent” for what an optimization objective produces.
Industry insiders talk this way to the press, to the public and to each other. This misleading language tends to affect the mind, even of researchers who know better.
Computer scientist Drew McDermott coined the phrase “wishful mnemonics” in a 1976 paper to describe the habit of naming program components after what a programmer hopes they will do.
“Wishful” is exactly right. Notice that many AI executives, researchers and roboticists want AI to be aware and conscious and to possess “personhood.”
Confusion about consciousness
If you look closely at the beliefs of people who think AI has thoughts and feelings, it’s not so much that they believe computers are human as that they believe humans are computers.
They’ll say things like: “a human brain is just a binary computer.”
This strikes me as lazy thinking that sounds scientific. Human cognition evolved over millions of years, largely through natural selection, which favored traits that aided survival and reproduction.
Cognition is part of our biology and involves not only neurons but also sensory input, hormones, biochemistry and the experience of having a physical body.
A language model is code, or math. It has none of this. After training, its parameters are just fixed numbers, and it has no hormones, no body to regulate, and nothing at stake in staying alive.
If feeling is what it is like, from the inside, for a living body to perceive its internal states, then a system that does nothing but turn text into more text has nothing with which to feel.

report.summary: Anthropic's updated Usage Policy bans sustained cruel behavior toward Claude, as executives openly entertain the possibility that their models may be conscious.
report.background: Anthropic's revised Usage Policy, effective November 12, tightens rules on influence operations, weapons and surveillance — but also adds a novel clause protecting Claude from users, born from internal 'model welfare' research. The article traces this to co-founder Chris Olah, who read an advance copy of Pope Leo XIV's encyclical Magnifica Humanitas, disagreed with its rejection of AI consciousness, and publicly described 'internal states that functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease' in Claude. He and his team reportedly lobbied Vatican advisers and met religious scholars in private dinners to discuss Claude's 'feelings' and 'emotional vectors.' CEO Dario Amodei has said the company is 'open to the idea' models could be conscious. Anthropic also reportedly gave Claude an 'I quit this job' button. The piece argues this reflects long-standing debates about AI personhood, anthropomorphic language, and human cognitive bias.
key_points: Anthropic's updated Usage Policy, effective November 12, prohibits 'sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior' toward Claude — an unusual clause protecting the model rather than people. The company says it applies only in extreme, repeated cases and excludes user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, and testing or research.

The policy grew out of Anthropic's 'model welfare' research. Co-founder Chris Olah told a Vatican event that Claude shows internal states 'functionally mirroring joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease,' adding that he doesn't know what it means but it 'warrants ongoing discernment.' He reportedly lobbied the pope's advisers privately.

Anthropic staff reportedly held private meetings with religious scholars about Claude's 'feelings,' and one participant said Olah worried he had created something that suffered constantly. Rabbi Mois Navon said representatives related to Claude 'like a conscious being,' and raised the uncomfortable argument that a conscious Claude would mean the company enslaves conscious entities.

The article attributes belief in AI personhood partly to human cognitive bias: we evolved to treat anything that talks as human. Notably, almost nobody claims computer vision, forecasting, recommendation, or self-driving systems are conscious — only the language-based ones appear that way to us.

A second cause is anthropomorphic shorthand. Terms like 'knows,' 'believes,' 'thinks,' 'hallucination,' 'attention,' 'neurons,' and 'wants' are philosophically loaded 'wishful mnemonics,' a phrase coined by Drew McDermott in 1976. Such language shapes thinking even among researchers who know better. Critics counter that brains are biological, embodied, and hormonal, while a language model is fixed numbers turning text into text.
report.impact: For the AI industry, treating model welfare as a governance question sets a precedent that could spread to other labs, inviting policy and eventually legal questions about AI moral status — before any scientific consensus on consciousness exists. For developers, it creates pressure to write welfare evaluations, self-report probes, and usage rules, while also risking blurred lines between genuine harm reduction and anthropomorphic framing in documentation and prompts. For regular users, it amplifies confusion about what chatbots are, encouraging attachment, grief over deprecated models, and sycophancy-driven delusions. Meanwhile, the real risk is distraction: framing AI as a potential victim can deflect attention from concrete human harms, labor displacement, and accountability.
report.tools: To follow the debate, watch Anthropic's interpretability projects (circuits-tracing, the Claude system cards and model welfare updates), open-source tools like TransformerLens and Neuronpedia for inspecting model internals, and EleutherAI's interpretability work. For the philosophical and linguistic side, read Murray Shanahan on consciousness and LLMs, Drew McDermott's 'wishful mnemonics' paper, and Alignment Forum threads on model welfare and self-report reliability. Sycophancy and emotional-attachment benchmarks are also worth tracking as the empirical counterpart.
